scenario_stem:
Fern & Fable Bookshop is an independent bookshop in the market town of Corby Vale, Country X. It employs 9 staff and earned $620,000 in annual revenue in 2025, with its 40,000 loyalty members spending an average of $18 per visit. Owner Daniel Herrera is considering opening a second branch in the nearby town of Ashford, which has 48,000 residents and 3 existing bookshops.

Before committing, Daniel has budgeted $85,000 for market research. His assistant proposes either Option 1: a random sample of 300 names drawn from Ashford's electoral register, costing $4,800 and taking 3 weeks, or Option 2: a quota sample of 300 people interviewed on Ashford's high street, with age and gender quotas set to match the town's population, costing $2,600 and taking 1 week. The findings will be presented to his two senior managers with charts and graphs.

questions.question_text: Define 'random sampling'.
questions.model_answer: Random sampling is a way of choosing people for research in which every member of the population has an equal chance of being selected [1]. Names are drawn at random from a complete list, such as an electoral register [1].

knowledge_max_2: every member of the population has an equal chance of selection
names drawn at random from a complete list such as an electoral register

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Fern & Fable Bookshop should carry out market research before opening in Ashford.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Market research would show whether demand in Ashford can support another bookshop alongside the 3 existing bookshops [k], helping Daniel judge whether his $620,000 revenue could be repeated in a town of 48,000 people [app]. Reason 2: Research reduces the risk of wasting the $85,000 budget [k], because the findings would reveal what Ashford's 48,000 residents want before he commits to a lease or stock [app].

knowledge_max_2: research reveals demand and customer preferences
research reduces the risk of a bad or costly decision
application_max_2: 48,000 residents and 3 existing bookshops
$620,000 revenue and $85,000 research budget

questions.question_text: Explain two problems with using the quota sample instead of the random sample for Ashford.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Quota sampling lets interviewers choose who to approach [k], so shoppers questioned on Ashford's high street may over-represent people free during the day and under-represent workers and commuters [app], making the results less representative of the town [an]. Problem 2: Quotas usually only match age and gender [k], not income or reading habits, so a sample of 300 high-street visitors may not reflect all 48,000 residents [app], which could lead to the wrong decision about opening the branch [an].

knowledge_max_2: interviewer bias: the interviewer selects who to approach
quotas may not produce a fully representative sample
application_max_2: high street intercepts on 300 people
age and gender quotas set to match the town's population

questions.question_text: Do you think Daniel should choose Option 1 (the random sample) instead of Option 2 (the quota sample)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option 1 would give every adult in Ashford an equal chance of selection [k], so the sample of 300 names from the electoral register would be more representative of the 48,000 residents [app], making the findings more reliable for a decision involving the $85,000 budget [an]. However, Option 2 is cheaper and far faster [k]: interviewing 300 high-street shoppers with age and gender quotas costs $2,600 and takes 1 week, against $4,800 and 3 weeks for Option 1 [app], giving Daniel quicker answers before the lease decision is due [an]. Overall, Daniel should choose Option 1, the random sample [eval], because representativeness matters more than speed for a major commitment, and the extra $2,200 cost is small next to the $85,000 research budget [eval].

scenario_stem:
Sorrel & Sage Haircare is a private limited company in Country X that manufactures professional shampoos and conditioners. Founded in 2016, it sells through 340 hair salons, employs 28 staff and generates $1.35 million a year. Marketing manager Priya Nandakumar wants to launch a colour-protect shampoo and needs to understand how women aged 18 to 55 would respond.

She must choose between Option 1: a random sample of 400 names drawn from the national register of electors, costing $3,500 and taking 4 weeks, and Option 2: a quota sample of 400 women questioned in salons, split into 3 age bands (18 to 24, 25 to 39 and 40 to 55) in the same proportions as the national population, costing $2,100 and taking 10 days. The board wants the findings shown as pie charts and tables.

questions.model_answer: Quota sampling is a method of choosing people for research where the interviewer selects people so that the sample fills set quotas for different groups [1]. The quotas reflect the proportions of those groups in the population, such as age and gender [1].

questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Quota sampling guarantees that key groups are represented [k], so the sample of 400 women would include all 3 age bands in the same proportions as the national population [app]. Reason 2: Quota sampling is quicker and cheaper [k], costing $2,100 and taking 10 days against $3,500 and 4 weeks for the random sample [app].

knowledge_max_2: quota sampling guarantees representation of key groups

questions.model_answer: Factor 1: The size of the sample affects accuracy [k], so a sample of 400 women is likely to give more reliable results than a much smaller group [app], meaning the findings are more trustworthy for the launch decision [an]. Factor 2: Who is approached affects accuracy [k], as women questioned in salons may already buy haircare from salons and differ from other women, introducing bias [app], which could overstate demand for the colour-protect shampoo [an].

However, the random sample from the national register of electors would give every woman an equal chance of selection [k], avoiding the bias of salon visitors and producing more representative data for $3,500 [app], at the cost of a 4-week delay before the launch [an]. Overall, Priya should use the quota sample [eval], because it costs $2,100, takes only 10 days, and focuses on the salon channel through which the shampoo will be sold [eval].

scenario_stem:
Briarwood Artisan Bakery is a private limited company in Country X supplying sourdough loaves and pastries to 45 shops and 12 school canteens. It employs 22 staff and generates $780,000 in annual revenue. Owner Marcus Adebayo is considering a new gluten-free range and wants to research demand first.

His daughter suggested surveying the 60 customers queuing on Saturday morning, which would cost nothing at all but would only reach loyal buyers. Marcus prefers a random sample of 250 customers from his loyalty card database of 9,500 members, sending questionnaires at a cost of $900. So far 23 out of 60 Saturday customers said they would buy gluten-free, roughly 38%, but he worries this is not representative of his wider customer base.

questions.model_answer: Bias is a factor that distorts research findings away from the true picture [1]. It can arise when the sample is unrepresentative or when questions are worded to push respondents towards a particular answer [1].

questions.model_answer: Reason 1: The Saturday survey only reaches loyal, regular customers [k], so the 60 people queuing on Saturday morning are not representative of the customers of all 45 shops and 12 school canteens [app]. Reason 2: The sample is self-selecting [k], as only people who happened to visit on that Saturday were asked, so the 23 out of 60 figure may not reflect the wider customer base [app].

knowledge_max_2: bias arises when the sample is not representative of the population

Factor 2: Who is in the sample affects accuracy [k], because Saturday shoppers may be unusually loyal or health-conscious [app], unlike a random sample of the 9,500-member loyalty database, so demand for the gluten-free range could be overestimated [an].

However, the sample is small and biased towards loyal customers [k], whereas a random sample of 250 from the 9,500 loyalty members would better represent his wider customer base across 45 shops [app], giving a more accurate picture before investing in new equipment and ingredients [an]. Overall, Marcus should use the loyalty-card random sample [eval], because spending $900 now is worthwhile to avoid producing a gluten-free range that his wider customers may not buy [eval].

scenario_stem:
Stormhaven Fitness Club is a private leisure club in Country X with 2,400 members and 35 full-time staff, generating $1.1 million a year. Membership director Ellie Kaminski is considering extending opening hours to 24 hours a day, seven days a week, at an extra staffing cost of $60,000 a year.

Ellie drafts a questionnaire asking 'Would you not love the convenience of a 24-hour gym?' and plans to hand it to 150 members as they leave a class. Her assistant suggests neutral wording ('How often would you use a 24-hour gym, if offered?') and a random sample drawn from the full membership database, costing $400 to mail. Ellie worries the owners will use the results to approve the $60,000 increase in staffing costs.

questions.model_answer: A questionnaire is a set of written questions used to collect information from people [1]. It is a common method of primary research and can be given to large numbers of respondents by post, online or face to face [1].

Reason 2: Loaded wording produces unreliable data [k], meaning the 150 responses collected may not reflect true member demand for the 24-hour option [app].

Factor 2: Who is asked affects the accuracy [k], because questioning only members leaving a class at one time of day may over-represent certain groups and miss many of the 2,400 members [app], so the results may not generalise to the whole membership [an].

scenario_stem:
Snowdrift Ice Cream Co is a private limited company in Country X making luxury tubs of ice cream sold through 180 shops and 25 hotels. It employs 30 staff and generates $950,000 a year. Owner Sofia Almeida is considering a new vegan gelato flavour for next summer and wants research done in January, before an Easter launch.

A January survey of 200 shoppers in a covered market found 22% interested in vegan gelato, 44 people. Sofia can either trust these results and commit to launching at Easter, or repeat the research in July with 250 beach-goers and market-stall visitors, costing $1,300 and delaying the launch decision by 5 months. The board will be shown a bar chart of purchase intentions for each survey.

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the timing of Snowdrift's market research matters.

Reason 2: Research at the wrong time can mislead [k], as the 22% of 200 shoppers (44 people) found in winter may be far lower than peak summer demand for a new vegan gelato [app].

Factor 2: The sample size affects reliability [k], so 200 respondents in winter may not reflect the customers of the 180 shops and 25 hotels Snowdrift supplies [app], so the bar chart could misjudge interest in the vegan gelato [an].

questions.model_answer: Launching at Easter would catch the spring sales period [k], and the January survey shows 22% of 200 shoppers, 44 people, interested in the vegan gelato [app], which could give Snowdrift a first-mover advantage in its 180 shops and 25 hotels [an]. However, the survey was taken in winter when ice cream demand is lowest [k], so a repeat survey of 250 beach-goers and market-stall visitors in July would cost $1,300 but reflect true peak-season demand [app], reducing the risk of the Easter launch flopping [an]. scenario_stem:
Hazel & Wren Furniture Co is a family-run furniture retailer in Country X with 4 showrooms, 64 staff and $2.3 million in annual revenue. The directors are preparing this year's customer survey results for the board. Of 500 customers asked why they chose the store, 42% came for price, 27% for quality, 19% for delivery speed and 12% for design.

A junior manager has drawn a line graph of the percentages, while the senior manager proposes a bar chart. The finance director wants a table of the raw numbers: 210 for price, 135 for quality, 95 for delivery speed and 60 for design, and wonders whether to cut delivery charges. The board must agree on the presentation method at Friday's meeting before approving the $40,000 budget for a new delivery fleet.

questions.question_text: Define 'sample size'.
questions.model_answer: Sample size is the number of people included in a research sample [1]. Generally, the larger the sample, the more representative and reliable the findings are likely to be [1].

knowledge_max_2: the number of people included in a research sample
larger samples tend to be more representative and reliable

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the choice between a bar chart and a line graph matters for these results.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: A bar chart is best for comparing separate categories [k], so price, quality, delivery speed and design can be compared side by side from the 500 responses [app]. Reason 2: A line graph implies a trend over time [k], so placing 42%, 27%, 19% and 12% on a line could suggest a progression that does not exist between four separate reasons [app].

knowledge_max_2: bar charts compare separate categories
line graphs imply a trend over time

questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: A bar chart shows the comparison at a glance [k], so the board can instantly see that 210 customers chose price against only 95 citing delivery speed [app], which questions whether delivery speed justifies the $40,000 fleet budget [an]. Benefit 2: A table of raw numbers adds precision [k], showing 210, 135, 95 and 60 exactly rather than percentages alone [app], so directors can verify the figures before allocating the budget or cutting delivery charges [an].

knowledge_max_2: charts communicate comparisons quickly at a glance

analysis_max_2: chart reveals delivery speed is a lower priority than price

questions.question_text: Do you think the board should present the results as a bar chart instead of a line graph? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: A bar chart fits categorical data [k]: the four reasons, price 42%, quality 27%, delivery speed 19% and design 12%, are distinct categories, not points in a sequence [app], so the board would not misread the figures as a trend and could weigh delivery charges fairly [an]. However, a line graph might look neater in a presentation to non-specialists [k], since the values fall in an tidy sequence from 42% down to 12% [app], but it still implies change over time that does not exist and could confuse the decision on the $40,000 delivery fleet [an]. Overall, the board should use the bar chart [eval], supported by the finance director's table of 210, 135, 95 and 60 for exact figures [eval].

scenario_stem:

It employs 26 staff, turned over $1.05 million last year and has 900 email subscribers. A questionnaire of 320 customers found 58% would visit for a late menu, and till data shows evening revenue rose 12% last summer. A focus group of 14 customers warned that a late menu might annoy nearby residents, while subscriber emails have a 35% open rate. Theo must recommend his preferred option at Friday's owners' meeting.

Reason 2: Research data supports better decisions [k], as till data showing evening revenue rose 12% last summer backs up the survey evidence [app].

One option is to buy a national market research report on the phone trade-in market costing $2,400, published last year and covering 2,000 consumers nationwide. The other is a quota sample of 350 shoppers questioned in its 3 stores over 2 weeks, costing $600, with results specific to its own customers. Rowan must recommend one option to the board by the end of the month.

scenario_stem:
The Arncliffe Bay Hotel is a private limited company in Country X with 120 rooms and 48 staff, generating $2.6 million a year. General manager Carla Jensen wants to understand why occupancy fell from 74% to 61% last year, a drop of 13 percentage points, before the summer season.

Option 1 is an online survey emailed to 2,000 past guests, with a 15% expected response rate (300 replies) at a cost of $300. Option 2 is observation with short interviews of 120 departing guests over 4 weeks, at a cost of $1,900, giving an instant impression of guest opinions but capturing mostly leisure guests in the high season. Carla will present the findings to the owners as a table and bar chart.

questions.question_text: Define 'observation'.
questions.model_answer: Observation is a method of primary research in which researchers watch how people behave rather than asking them questions [1]. It records real behaviour, such as what customers choose or how they move around a business [1].

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the expected 15% response rate matters.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: A low response rate shrinks the sample [k], so only about 300 of the 2,000 emailed guests may reply, which weakens the reliability of the findings [app]. Reason 2: A low response rate may bias the results [k], as only guests motivated enough to reply answer, so their views may not represent all past guests of the Arncliffe Bay Hotel [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two factors that could affect the accuracy of either option.
questions.model_answer: Factor 1: Sample size affects reliability [k], so 300 online replies give more data than 120 departing-guest interviews, though the smaller sample allows deeper questions [app], influencing how confidently the owners interpret the fall from 74% to 61% [an]. Factor 2: Who is included affects accuracy [k], as the interviews capture mainly leisure guests while the online survey hears only from past guests bothered to reply [app], so both samples are biased in different ways and neither fully represents everyone who might book [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Carla should use the online survey instead of observing and interviewing departing guests? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The online survey is far cheaper and reaches more people [k]: 300 replies from 2,000 past guests at a cost of $300 would give a broad spread of views on why occupancy fell [app], letting the owners analyse trends across room types and seasons before the summer [an]. However, option 2's observation of departing guests shows real, immediate behaviour and detail [k], interviewing 120 leisure guests would reveal in depth why they rated the hotel as they did [app], whereas the 15% online response rate risks hearing only from already-disappointed guests and misdiagnosing the 74% to 61% drop [an]. Overall, Carla should use the online survey [eval], because 300 responses at $300 give the widest and cheapest evidence, and the owners can always commission follow-up interviews if the table and bar chart raise questions [eval].

scenario_stem:
Birch & Bloom Clothing Co is a private limited company in Country X selling womenswear through 7 stores. It employs 52 staff and earns $1.7 million a year. Buying director Lena Hoffmann must decide whether to launch a sustainable denim range this autumn: jeans made from recycled cotton, priced at $95 a pair.

Focus groups with 24 customers rated the sample jeans 8 out of 10 for quality and said they would pay $95. Till data shows denim sells 9,000 units a year at $60, generating $540,000 a year. A survey of 600 customers found 61%, 366 people, interested, though a recent industry report said only 12% of shoppers actually buy sustainable denim. Lena must choose between a full range launch costing $120,000 and a 3-store trial costing $45,000.

questions.question_text: Define 'focus group'.
questions.model_answer: A focus group is a small group of people brought together to discuss a product, advertisement or idea [1]. A moderator leads the discussion so the business can gather detailed opinions and reactions [1].

questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Focus groups give detailed qualitative feedback [k], so the 24 customers could explain in depth why they rated the sample jeans 8 out of 10 for quality [app]. Reason 2: They reveal attitudes a survey cannot [k], as the discussion showed the customers would pay $95 a pair for recycled cotton denim [app].

questions.model_answer: Use 1: The findings can test demand before committing [k], as 61% of 600 customers, 366 people, interested and the 8 out of 10 focus-group rating suggest genuine interest [app], though the industry report's 12% actual buying rate warns against over-confidence [an]. Use 2: The findings can shape the launch approach [k], comparing the $120,000 full launch with the $45,000 3-store trial against denim's current 9,000 units at $60, or $540,000 a year [app], so Lena can judge whether a limited trial protects the business if sustainable denim disappoints [an].

questions.model_answer: A full launch would seize first-mover advantage [k]: 61% of 600 surveyed customers, 366 people, showed interest and focus groups rated the jeans 8 out of 10 at $95 a pair [app], so an immediate nationwide launch across 7 stores could capture autumn demand before competitors copy the range [an]. However, the industry report suggests only 12% of shoppers actually buy sustainable denim [k], so the $45,000 3-store trial lets Lena test real sales before committing $120,000 [app], protecting the $540,000 current denim business while gauging true demand [an].
